stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to your practice with 6 migraine episodes per month over the past 4 months. Each episode lasts 24 hours, causes her to miss work, and responds partially to oral sumatriptan 50 mg. She has no aura. Her past medical history includes moderate persistent asthma well-controlled on Symbicort maintenance and reliever. She has no depression, no cardiac history, and no pregnancy plans over the next 12 months.

Her only regular medications are Symbicort and paracetamol as needed. She does not use oral contraception. She has trialled magnesium 400 mg daily for 3 months without benefit. She has identified triggers of poor sleep and skipping meals which she is addressing with sleep hygiene and structured eating.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; cranial nerve exam within normal limits; no focal neurology; fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TSH, UEC within normal limits; no imaging indicated by red flag review

lead_in: What is the most appropriate migraine prophylaxis to commence?

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg twice daily titrated to 80 mg twice daily over 4 weeks as needed
options.rationale: Propranolol is usually first-line migraine prophylaxis, but is relatively contraindicated in moderate persistent asthma and a non-cardioselective beta-blocker may worsen bronchospasm. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine

options.text: Continue current sumatriptan and add regular paracetamol daily as prophylaxis at home
options.rationale: Regular daily paracetamol risks medication overuse headache and is not effective prophylaxis; prophylactic therapy needs a targeted evidence-based agent. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine

options.text: Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1500 mg total daily dose over 4 weeks
options.rationale: Valproate is effective for migraine prophylaxis but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age unless pregnancy prevention criteria are strictly met due to teratogenicity risk. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine

options.text: Verapamil 80 mg three times daily as prophylaxis with cardiac ECG at baseline before start
options.rationale: Verapamil is used for cluster headache prophylaxis rather than migraine; it lacks the evidence base of TCAs, beta-blockers or topiramate for migraine. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine

options.text: Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated up to 25 to 50 mg nocte over 4 to 6 weeks as tolerated
options.rationale: In a patient where beta-blocker is unsuitable (moderate persistent asthma), amitriptyline is a preferred first-line migraine prophylactic per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4 or more monthly migraine days, or fewer episodes that significantly impair function. Australian eTG first-line agents are propranolol (first-line if no contraindication), amitriptyline (preferred if asthma, comorbid tension headache or insomnia), topiramate, sodium valproate (contraindicated in women of childbearing age without strict pregnancy prevention), pizotifen and candesartan. Newer CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are PBS-listed for refractory chronic migraine after failure of 3 prior classes. Trial each agent for 8-12 weeks at target dose before considering failure.
key_points: Prophylaxis threshold: 4+ migraine days per month or significant impairment.
Propranolol is first-line unless asthma, brady, hypotension.
Amitriptyline is preferred with asthma or insomnia comorbidity.
Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing age.
explanation.pearls: Frequent migraine in an asthmatic woman: skip propranolol, choose amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated to 25-50 mg; trial for 8-12 weeks before deeming ineffective.

sources.label: Australian Headache Society: Migraine management position statement

stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents to your practice with 12 months of progressive central weight gain (9 kg), easy bruising on her arms with minimal trauma, new-onset hypertension requiring a second agent, oligomenorrhoea and mood lability. Her mother had breast cancer at 62. She has striae 8 mm wide across her abdomen and flanks that are purple. She takes amlodipine 5 mg and irbesartan 150 mg for blood pressure.

She has no exogenous glucocorticoid use, including no inhaled or intra-articular steroids. She drinks 1 to 2 standard drinks per week and does not shift-work. Random morning cortisol taken by another practitioner was 480 nmol/L. Fasting glucose is 6.8 mmol/L, and HbA1c is 6.5 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two agents, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity with dorsocervical fat pad; wide purple striae on abdomen and flanks; proximal muscle weakness; easy bruising on arms
data_table.Investigations: Random morning cortisol 480 nmol/L; fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 6.5 percent; potassium 3.6 mmol/L; no exogenous steroid use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line screening investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with morning cortisol at 08:00 the next day
options.rationale: 1 mg overnight DST is a preferred Endocrine Society and Australian first-line screen for suspected Cushing syndrome; a morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L suggests failure of suppression and warrants further investigation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline

options.text: Plasma ACTH measurement in a single early morning sample as the initial screening test
options.rationale: ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after diagnosis is established, not as a screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline

options.text: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of ACTH secretion definitively
options.rationale: IPSS is a highly specialised test for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH after Cushing is confirmed and ACTH-dependent aetiology established. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline

options.text: Random single serum cortisol interpreted against a fixed cut-off value of 500 nanomole/L
options.rationale: Random cortisol is unreliable due to diurnal variation; screening uses 1 mg DST, 24 hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline

options.text: CT of the adrenal glands and pituitary MRI before any biochemical confirmation is undertaken
options.rationale: Imaging before biochemistry generates incidentaloma noise (adrenal nodules are common); biochemical confirmation must come first. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome is investigated stepwise: confirm hypercortisolism biochemically before any imaging or localisation. First-line screening tests (any two positive out of three, or one strongly positive with high clinical suspicion) are 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression (cortisol under 50 nmol/L excludes), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (2-3 collections), and late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm). Once confirmed, plasma ACTH distinguishes ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) aetiology, then imaging directs pituitary vs ectopic vs adrenal disease. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for ACTH-dependent cases with equivocal pituitary MRI.
key_points: Confirm hypercortisolism before any imaging.
1 mg DST, 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary are screens.
ACTH after confirmation distinguishes dependent from independent.
IPSS for equivocal ACTH-dependent pituitary MRI.
explanation.pearls: Suspected Cushing: start with 1 mg overnight DST and 08:00 cortisol; only after confirmed hypercortisolism measure ACTH and image.

stem:
A 68-year-old male ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 8 years ago) presents to your respiratory outpatient clinic with 12 months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He has bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. His FVC is 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, and DLCO is 42 percent predicted.

He has no rash, joint symptoms, or Raynaud's phenomenon. Autoimmune serology (ANA, ENA, anti-CCP, RF, MPO, PR3) is negative. He has never worked in mining, construction or with asbestos. HRCT chest today shows peripheral and basal reticulation with honeycombing 5 mm subpleural cysts and traction bronchiectasis, with no ground glass and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles; finger clubbing; no rash; no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FVC 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, DLCO 42 percent predicted; autoimmune serology negative; HRCT: definite UIP pattern with honeycombing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Empirical high-dose prednisolone 60 mg daily for 6 weeks to arrest disease progression
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy does not benefit IPF and may harm; antifibrotic therapy is the standard. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Refer to a specialist ILD multidisciplinary team for antifibrotic therapy consideration
options.rationale: A definite UIP pattern on HRCT in a clinical context of IPF meets AU criteria to refer for antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) via a specialist ILD service. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Surgical lung biopsy from the right lower lobe to obtain definitive tissue diagnosis first
options.rationale: Definite UIP pattern on HRCT in the appropriate clinical context does not require surgical biopsy per current AU guidance; biopsy is reserved for probable or indeterminate UIP. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily as antioxidant monotherapy for slow progression
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine monotherapy in IPF was not superior to placebo (PANTHER-IPF) and is not recommended. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Reassurance and 12-month observation with repeat HRCT to confirm progression before treatment
options.rationale: IPF is progressive; deferring antifibrotic therapy allows irreversible loss of function which cannot be recovered. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive fibrotic interstitial lung disease diagnosed by an ILD multidisciplinary team using HRCT and clinical assessment. Definite UIP pattern on HRCT (basal and peripheral reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, no atypical features) in an appropriate clinical context does not require surgical lung biopsy. Antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slows FVC decline and is PBS-listed for FVC 50-80 percent predicted and DLCO 30-79 percent predicted. Non-pharmacological care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, smoking cessation, oxygen for hypoxaemia, vaccinations, and early lung transplant referral for suitable candidates.
key_points: Definite HRCT UIP + clinical context = IPF diagnosis without biopsy.
Antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slow FVC decline.
PBS criteria: FVC 50-80 and DLCO 30-79 predicted.
Steroids and NAC monotherapy not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Definite UIP on HRCT with FVC 68 and DLCO 42 in a clinical IPF phenotype: refer to ILD MDT for pirfenidone or nintedanib; do not use steroids or NAC as primary therapy.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

stem:
A 66-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of fever, productive cough, pleuritic left-sided chest pain and confusion. He usually lives independently and manages his own affairs but today he cannot recall the day of the week. He has stage 3 CKD (baseline creatinine 150 micromol/L) and hypertension.

On examination he has bronchial breathing at the left lower zone and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. SMART-COP score is 5. His lactate is 3.4 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L. Blood cultures have been taken. He is not immunosuppressed and has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 89 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: New confusion (AMT 6/10); bronchial breathing left lower zone with dullness to percussion; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 240 mg/L; lactate 3.4 mmol/L; creatinine 220 micromol/L; blood cultures pending; CXR left lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic combination?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 1 g plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily now
options.rationale: For severe CAP with SMART-COP 5 and organ dysfunction, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the Australian eTG regimen rather than amoxicillin plus gentamicin. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g plus oral doxycycline 100 mg for community treatment at home tonight
options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 mandates inpatient IV therapy with ICU review; oral outpatient treatment is unsafe. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg then IV fluid resuscitation and reassessment
options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 defines severe CAP requiring ICU-capable care; the Australian eTG severe CAP regimen is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (or moxifloxacin monotherapy if beta-lactam allergy). (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g plus IV vancomycin as broad-spectrum first-line therapy
options.rationale: Broad Gram negative and MRSA cover is not first-line for community-acquired pneumonia; ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers typical and atypical pathogens. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g monotherapy every 8 hours for empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial cover
options.rationale: Meropenem is inappropriate first-line for CAP; it drives selection pressure for resistance and is reserved for hospital-acquired or resistant infection. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

explanation.summary: Australian severity-stratified community-acquired pneumonia (SMART-COP: Systolic BP under 90, Multilobar CXR, Albumin under 35, Respiratory rate raised, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygenation low, pH under 7.35) directs treatment intensity. SMART-COP 5 or above signals severe disease requiring ICU-capable care and dual IV antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (or benzylpenicillin) plus IV azithromycin 500 mg daily to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia). Moxifloxacin monotherapy is an alternative for beta-lactam allergy. Sepsis hour-1 bundle includes lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor if not fluid-responsive.
key_points: SMART-COP 5+ triggers severe CAP pathway.
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin.
Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid.
Moxifloxacin monotherapy for severe beta-lactam allergy.
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP 5 with lactate 3.4 mandates IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg within the sepsis hour; cultures first, then antibiotics, then 30 mL/kg crystalloid.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 24 hours of fever, right flank pain, dysuria and urinary frequency. She has vomited once but tolerates oral fluids and food now. She has no relevant past medical history and takes no regular medications. She is not pregnant (recent period 10 days ago, contraception with the LNG-IUS in situ).

On examination she has right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness without peritonism. Urinalysis shows blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent. She has social supports at home and can attend for reassessment at 48 hours if needed. She is not systemically septic - HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 18, SpO2 99, temperature 38.4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen soft with right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness; no peritonism; genitalia unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days at home with a review at 48 hours in clinic
options.rationale: Trimethoprim short course treats uncomplicated cystitis not pyelonephritis; pyelonephritis requires an oral fluoroquinolone or cefalexin equivalent for 10 to 14 days. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 7 days from your general practice today
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations for pyelonephritis and is restricted to cystitis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV ampicillin every 6 hours until afebrile 48 hours
options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for severe sepsis, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral, or failure of oral therapy; she is systemically well and tolerating fluids. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days with clinic review at 48 hours from now
options.rationale: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a systemically well adult who tolerates oral intake is managed as an outpatient with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as first-line empirical antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Amoxicillin resistance rates in E coli exceed 50 percent and empirical amoxicillin monotherapy is inadequate for pyelonephritis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult who is systemically well and can tolerate oral fluids is managed as an outpatient per Australian eTG. First-line oral therapy is ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength) BD for 14 days if fluoroquinolone contraindicated. Cefalexin 500 mg QID for 14 days is an alternative. Admission for IV therapy is required for severe sepsis, pregnancy, uncontrolled vomiting, urinary tract obstruction (needs urgent drainage), or failure of oral therapy at 48 hours. Urine culture guides definitive therapy; imaging (renal ultrasound or CT) is reserved for recurrent infection, poor response or suspected obstruction.
key_points: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days.
Admission for IV: severe sepsis, pregnancy, vomiting, obstruction.
Trimethoprim short course is for cystitis only.
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis.
explanation.pearls: Well non-pregnant adult with pyelonephritis who tolerates oral fluids: outpatient ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days with 48 hour review; admit if severe sepsis, pregnancy or ongoing vomiting.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection
Cochrane 2010: Antibiotic regimens for acute pyelonephritis

stem:
A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden severe headache and left-sided weakness. Her CT brain shows a right-sided intracerebral haemorrhage in the basal ganglia measuring 35 mm with mild midline shift. Her INR on arrival is 3.8.

She is drowsy but rousable, moving all four limbs with 3/5 power on the left and 5/5 on the right. She was last stable INR 3 weeks ago at 2.6. Her regular medications also include perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. She has no known drug allergies. She weighs 68 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 176/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3V4M6); left hemiparesis 3/5; right side 5/5; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.8; APTT 42 sec; platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 92 micromol/L; CT brain: 35 mm right basal ganglia ICH with mild midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa) as a single bolus dose given intravenously today
options.rationale: rFVIIa is not routinely used for warfarin reversal; prothrombinex provides balanced factor replacement and is the AU standard. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
source_refs: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg oral only and observe INR trend for the next 6 hours prior to reassessment
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is too slow (24 to 48 hours to lower INR) for a life-threatening ICH; IV route and factor replacement are required. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
source_refs: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg IV alone as reversal without any additional intervention
options.rationale: FFP alone requires large volumes and delivers unpredictable factor levels; prothrombinex is preferred and provides faster INR correction. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
source_refs: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g IV as immediate warfarin reversal in the emergency department resuscitation
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; there is no role in warfarin-associated bleeding. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
source_refs: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg IV plus prothrombinex 50 units/kg IV given as soon as they can be prepared
options.rationale: Major bleeding on warfarin (any life-threatening or intracranial bleed) requires immediate reversal with IV vitamin K plus prothrombinex per Australian THANZ/AHRTC guidance; FFP alone is inadequate. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
source_refs: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding, including any intracranial haemorrhage or life-threatening bleed at any INR, requires immediate reversal per Australian THANZ consensus. The standard combination is IV vitamin K 10 mg (works over 6-24 hours) plus prothrombinex 25-50 units/kg (works within minutes to hours). Vitamin K provides sustained reversal by allowing hepatic synthesis of clotting factors; prothrombinex provides immediate factor II, VII, IX, X replacement. FFP is used only if prothrombinex is unavailable, at 15 mL/kg. Recheck INR at 30 minutes and repeat prothrombinex if INR remains above 1.5. Blood pressure control (systolic under 140) reduces haematoma expansion in ICH.
key_points: Warfarin major bleed: IV vitamin K + prothrombinex.
Vitamin K sustains reversal; prothrombinex is immediate.
FFP is a backup only when prothrombinex unavailable.
Idarucizumab is for dabigatran, andexanet for FXa inhibitors.
explanation.pearls: Warfarin ICH with INR 3.8: IV vitamin K 10 mg + prothrombinex 50 units/kg immediately; check INR at 30 min and target under 1.5; drop systolic BP to under 140 to limit expansion.
